statement: In the sponsor's pooled analysis of four phase 2 trials of MDMA-assisted psychotherapy for chronic PTSD, as corrected (correction published online in December 2024: four participants of one site, treated by two therapists involved in an ethical violation, were removed, and the journal issued an expression of concern because the authors had not disclosed the violation at submission), full-dose MDMA compared with low-dose MDMA with the same psychotherapy was associated with a larger improvement in self-reported sleep quality 1 to 2 months after two blinded sessions: change on the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (0 to 21, higher is worse) −3.5 against +0.5 points (Hedges' g 0.85, 95% CI 0.23 to 1.47; 44 and 14 participants), with an improvement of at least 3 points in 24 of 45 against 2 of 14. After open-label full-dose treatment for everyone, mean scores 12 months later were about 1 point lower than at the end of treatment (7.1 against 8.2), without a comparison group. The paper reports no check of whether participants could tell their dose, the outcome is self-reported, the analyses were not preregistered and the dose groups were defined partly after inspecting outcomes. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: In four early trials run for the same sponsor, people with PTSD who had full doses of MDMA said they slept better a month or two later than people who had a very small dose: about 4 points better on a 0 to 21 sleep scale. A year later their sleep was a little better still, but by then everyone had had full doses, so there was nothing to compare with. No one checked whether people could tell which dose they had, and the results had to be corrected after an ethics breach at one site.
population: Adults with chronic PTSD in four of the sponsor's phase 2 trials (59 after the correction: 45 full dose, 14 low dose)
exposure: Two blinded sessions with full-dose MDMA within manualized psychotherapy
comparator: Low-dose MDMA with the same psychotherapy (no inactive placebo after the correction)
outcome: Change in self-reported sleep quality (Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index) from baseline to 1 to 2 months after the blinded sessions; open-label change to 12 months
magnitude: Corrected blinded endpoint: PSQI change −3.51 (SD 5.08, n = 44) against +0.50 (3.25, n = 14), p = .008, Hedges' g 0.85 (95% CI 0.23 to 1.47); improvement of 3 points or more in 24 of 45 (53.3%) against 2 of 14 (14.3%). Corrected open-label, N = 58: PSQI least-squares means 12.59 at baseline, 8.18 at treatment exit, 7.09 at 12 months; exit to 12 months −1.09 (SE 0.49), p = .029. Original (superseded) analysis: −3.53 against +0.56, g 0.88, p = .003.

evidence.extracted: Original analysis, superseded by the correction: PSQI change −3.53 (SD 5.03) in the active group against +0.56 (3.05) in the control group (n = 16; active n printed as 46 in Table 2 and 47 elsewhere), p = .003, Hedges' g 0.88 with a printed 95% CI of −0.27 to 2.03 that does not fit g; a drop of 3 points or more in 53.2% against 12.5% (N = 61).

evidence.locator: Summary of corrections made › Blinded endpoint, 1st paragraph (revised text); corrected Table 2
evidence.extracted: Corrected blinded endpoint: PSQI change −3.51 (SD 5.08) in the active group (n = 44) against +0.50 (3.25) in the control group (n = 14), p = .008, Hedges' g 0.85 (95% CI 0.23 to 1.47); CAPS-IV −34.93 against −11.07, g 0.96 (0.33 to 1.59).

PSQI fell by 3 points or more in 24 active participants (53.3%, of 45) and 2 controls (14.3%, of 14), p = .008; the footnote's counts and denominators do not fully agree (19 active without such a drop, n = 44 in the table).
Open-label (N = 58): PSQI least-squares means 12.59 at baseline, 8.18 at treatment exit, 7.09 at 12 months; change from exit to 12 months −1.09 (SE 0.49), p = .029.

evidence.locator: Description and explanation for this correction; Summary of corrections made › In the abstract
evidence.extracted: The four MP-4 participants treated by the pair of therapists were removed; sample 63 to 59 (active 47 to 45, control 16 to 14); the removed participants were the only ones in the control group given no MDMA, so the control group now consists only of low-dose MDMA and the placebo label is dropped.

The authors had not notified the journal of the ethical violation at submission (December 2019), although it had been publicly announced in May 2019; the journal judged this improper and issued the expression of concern; its investigation of human-subjects ethics was inconclusive.

evidence.locator: Method › Data Analysis, 1st paragraph; Open Practices Statement
evidence.extracted: Doses pooled into control and active groups by the protocols' designations and by inspection of post-treatment CAPS-IV scores (citing the since-retracted pooled analysis by Mithoefer et al., 2019); independent-samples t tests; no power analysis; the analyses were not formally preregistered.

evidence.locator: Method › Measures › Sleep Quality, 1st paragraph; Discussion, 5th paragraph
evidence.extracted: Sleep quality was measured with the self-report PSQI (global score 0 to 21; a cut-off of 5 separates good from poor sleepers); the authors list the small, mostly White sample and self-reported outcomes as limitations; the paper reports no assessment of whether participants could tell their dose.

risk_of_bias.note: Very serious: self-reported outcome without any check of blinding; analysis not preregistered, with groups defined partly after inspecting outcomes and pooled without stratification; the data were corrected after an ethical violation at one site, under an expression of concern.

imprecision.note: 58 participants, 14 controls; the interval for g runs from 0.23 to 1.47.

grade.reasoning: The blinded comparison rests on randomization within each trial, so it starts high, but it is rated down twice for risk of bias (RoB 2 high on the study card: a self-reported outcome with no check of blinding, outcome-informed grouping, unstratified pooling, no preregistration, and the expression of concern) and once for imprecision. The relation is an association rather than a causal verb because the pooled comparison does not preserve each trial's randomization. The 12-month figures are uncontrolled and are given only as a description. This is one pooled analysis whose per-trial results are not reported, hence single study.
